title: Chronic coronary syndrome (stable angina)
subject: cardiology
summary: Estimate pre-test likelihood, then use CCTA (likelihood above 5 to 50%) or functional imaging (above 15 to 85%); give sublingual nitrate plus a beta-blocker and/or CCB, lifelong aspirin or clopidogrel, high-intensity statin to LDL-C below 55 mg/dL, and revascularise for refractory angina or high-risk anatomy (ESC 2024).

sections.title: Recognise
items: Typical angina: constricting chest, jaw, neck or arm discomfort brought on by exertion or emotional stress and relieved within minutes by rest or sublingual nitrate. Exertional breathlessness, dizziness or fatigue can be angina equivalents.
Exclude an acute coronary syndrome first: rest pain, a crescendo pattern or new severe angina needs the acute pathway with high-sensitivity troponin (see the NSTE-ACS protocol).
Grade severity with the Canadian Cardiovascular Society angina class (class I: angina only with strenuous exertion; class IV: angina with any physical activity or at rest).

Estimate the pre-test likelihood of obstructive CAD with the ESC Risk Factor-weighted Clinical Likelihood model (age, sex, symptom type, number of risk factors), then adjust it for ECG, echo, peripheral artery disease or known vascular calcification.

Consider other causes of angina: aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, tachyarrhythmia, and ANOCA/INOCA (microvascular or vasospastic angina) when the coronary arteries are non-obstructive.

sections.title: Diagnostic pathway
items: All patients: resting 12-lead ECG, FBC (haemoglobin), creatinine with eGFR, lipid profile with LDL-C, HbA1c or fasting glucose, and thyroid function at least once.
Resting transthoracic echo for LVEF, regional wall motion, valve disease (especially aortic stenosis), RV function and estimated pulmonary pressure.
Pre-test likelihood 5% or less: consider deferring further testing. Low likelihood (above 5 to 15%): a coronary artery calcium score can reclassify patients to very low likelihood.

Low to moderate likelihood (above 5 to 50%): CCTA is the preferred test to rule out obstructive CAD. Avoid CCTA with eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2, decompensated heart failure, fast irregular rhythm, extensive calcification or inability to breath-hold.
Moderate to high likelihood (above 15 to 85%): functional imaging (stress echo, SPECT or preferably PET perfusion, or stress CMR) to diagnose and quantify ischaemia.

Very high likelihood (above 85%), angina at a low workload, symptoms refractory to medical therapy or high event risk: invasive coronary angiography by radial access, with FFR (significant 0.80 or less) or iFR (0.89 or less) for intermediate stenoses.
Exercise ECG is not recommended to rule out CAD in low or moderate likelihood when CCTA or functional imaging is available; it still helps assess exercise tolerance, BP response and risk.

High-risk findings: ischaemia of 10% or more of the LV on SPECT or PET, 3 or more of 16 ischaemic segments on stress echo, left main stenosis of 50% or more, or three-vessel disease with 70% stenoses on CCTA.

sections.title: Antianginal therapy
items: Give every patient sublingual GTN for immediate relief (and before exertion). Repeat after 5 minutes if needed; call emergency services if pain persists 5 minutes after the second dose.
First line: a beta-blocker and/or a calcium-channel blocker (CCB), chosen by heart rate, BP, LV function, comorbidities, tolerability and cost.
If one agent fails, combine a beta-blocker with a dihydropyridine CCB (amlodipine). Avoid verapamil or diltiazem with a beta-blocker in bradycardia, AV block or reduced LVEF.

Add-on (or initial in selected patients): long-acting nitrate (for example isosorbide mononitrate MR 30 to 60 mg once daily, max 120 mg) with a nitrate-free interval, or ranolazine. Nicorandil or trimetazidine may also be considered.
Ivabradine only as add-on when LVEF is below 40% with inadequate symptom control; it is not recommended with LVEF above 40% and no heart failure.
Never combine ivabradine with verapamil, diltiazem or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. No nitrates in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or within 24 hours of sildenafil (48 hours of tadalafil).

sections.title: Preventing events
items: Aspirin 75 to 100 mg daily lifelong after MI or revascularisation, and in obstructive CAD without prior events. Clopidogrel 75 mg daily is a safe and effective alternative to aspirin.

After elective PCI: DAPT with aspirin 75 to 100 mg plus clopidogrel 75 mg daily for up to 6 months; 1 to 3 months in high bleeding risk (PRECISE-DAPT or ARC-HBR) without high ischaemic risk, then single antiplatelet.

High ischaemic risk and no high bleeding risk: consider adding a second agent to aspirin long term: rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily, ticagrelor 60 mg twice daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily or prasugrel 10 mg daily.

AF or other OAC indication: DOAC preferred to VKA. After PCI stop aspirin within 1 week (up to 1 month if high ischaemic risk), continue OAC plus clopidogrel up to 6 months (12 months if high ischaemic risk), then OAC alone. No ticagrelor or prasugrel in triple therapy.
High-intensity statin for all: target LDL-C below 55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L) and a reduction of at least 50%. Add ezetimibe, then a PCSK9 inhibitor; bempedoic acid if statin intolerant.
ACE inhibitor (or ARB) with hypertension, diabetes or heart failure. In type 2 diabetes, an SGLT2 inhibitor and a GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven CV benefit. Consider colchicine 0.5 mg daily.
PPI for patients at increased GI bleeding risk on combined antithrombotic therapy.

Risk factor targets: SBP 120 to 129 mmHg if tolerated, HbA1c below 7.0%, stop smoking, 150 to 300 minutes a week of moderate exercise, alcohol below 100 g a week, influenza and pneumococcal vaccination.

sections.title: Revascularisation
items: Persistent angina despite guideline-directed medical therapy: revascularise functionally significant obstructive CAD (PCI or CABG) to improve symptoms.
To improve outcomes (LVEF above 35%): functionally significant left main stenosis, three-vessel disease, or one- or two-vessel disease involving the proximal LAD.
Left main disease: CABG is preferred overall; PCI is an alternative when the SYNTAX score is 22 or less. Multivessel disease with diabetes: CABG over PCI.
LVEF 35% or less with multivessel CAD: CABG over medical therapy alone in surgical candidates, decided by the Heart Team.
Use a Heart Team for complex anatomy; calculate the SYNTAX score in multivessel disease and the STS score before CABG.
New rest pain, crescendo angina or syncope: manage as a possible acute coronary syndrome, same day.

sections.title: Special situations
items: ANOCA/INOCA: persistent angina with non-obstructive arteries and poor quality of life warrants invasive coronary function testing to identify microvascular angina or vasospasm.
Vasospastic angina (rest angina with transient ST change that resolves with nitrate): record an ECG during pain; treat with a CCB plus nitrate. Beta-blockers alone may aggravate spasm.
Heart failure with LVEF 40% or less: full GDMT (ACE-I or ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor); with LVEF 35% or less and suspected CAD, invasive angiography with a view to CABG.
Age 75 or older: watch for drug interactions, hypotension, bleeding and renal dosing; base decisions on symptoms, frailty, life expectancy and preferences.
Do not give postmenopausal hormone therapy to women with CCS.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Labelling new or accelerating chest pain as stable angina; it needs same-day assessment.
Using a normal exercise ECG to exclude CAD in intermediate-likelihood patients.
Missing severe aortic stenosis before starting nitrates or vasodilators: listen for an ejection systolic murmur and check the echo.
Stopping antiplatelet therapy early after stenting (stent thrombosis).
Nitrates with sildenafil or tadalafil (profound hypotension).
Not rechecking LDL-C after starting or changing lipid therapy and failing to escalate to reach the target.

drugs.name: Glyceryl trinitrate (GTN), sublingual
drugs.dose: 300 to 600 mcg tablet or 400 mcg spray (1 to 2 puffs) sublingually at onset; repeat after 5 minutes
drugs.notes: Also before exertion. Avoid with PDE5 inhibitors and in HCM with outflow obstruction.

drugs.name: Bisoprolol
drugs.dose: Start 2.5 to 5 mg orally once daily; titrate to 10 mg once daily (max 20 mg)
drugs.notes: Aim for a resting heart rate around 55 to 60 bpm. Avoid in marked bradycardia, high-grade AV block, decompensated heart failure.

drugs.name: Amlodipine
drugs.dose: 5 mg orally once daily, up to 10 mg once daily
drugs.notes: Safe to combine with a beta-blocker. Ankle oedema is common.

drugs.name: Ranolazine (prolonged release)
drugs.dose: 375 mg orally twice daily; after 2 to 4 weeks 500 mg twice daily, up to 750 mg twice daily
drugs.notes: Contraindicated with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, CrCl below 30 mL/min, moderate or severe hepatic impairment. Prolongs QT.

drugs.name: Ivabradine
drugs.dose: 5 mg orally twice daily (2.5 mg twice daily if 75 years or older); after 3 to 4 weeks up to 7.5 mg twice daily
drugs.notes: Sinus rhythm with resting HR 70 bpm or more and LVEF below 40%. Reduce if HR falls below 50 bpm. Not with verapamil or diltiazem.

drugs.name: Aspirin
drugs.dose: 75 to 100 mg orally once daily, lifelong
drugs.notes: Clopidogrel 75 mg daily if aspirin is not tolerated or as an equal alternative.

drugs.name: Clopidogrel
drugs.dose: 75 mg orally once daily (600 mg loading dose before elective PCI)
drugs.notes: Default P2Y12 inhibitor with aspirin for up to 6 months after elective PCI, and with an OAC after PCI.

drugs.name: Rivaroxaban (vascular dose)
drugs.dose: 2.5 mg orally twice daily with aspirin 75 to 100 mg once daily
drugs.notes: High ischaemic risk without high bleeding risk. Not an anticoagulant dose for AF or VTE.

drugs.name: Atorvastatin
drugs.dose: 40 to 80 mg orally once daily (or rosuvastatin 20 to 40 mg once daily)
drugs.notes: Target LDL-C below 55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L) and at least 50% reduction; add ezetimibe 10 mg daily if not at target.

drugs.name: Colchicine (low dose)
drugs.notes: Should be considered in atherosclerotic CAD. Avoid in severe renal or hepatic impairment and with strong CYP3A4 or P-gp inhibitors (for example clarithromycin).

algorithms.title: Chronic Coronary Syndrome Diagnostic and Antianginal Optimization Pathway

steps.action: Assess chest pain characteristics (typical vs atypical vs non-cardiac). Perform 12-lead resting ECG, baseline biochemistry, and resting echocardiography (assess LV ejection fraction and regional wall motion).
Calculate pre-test likelihood based on ESC 2024 age, sex, and symptom criteria. If PTP < 5%, defer non-invasive testing and investigate non-cardiac causes.

steps.branch: PTP 5% to 15% or Low Clinical Likelihood
steps.action: Coronary CT Angiography (CCTA) is preferred first-line to rule out anatomical obstructive CAD with high negative predictive value.

steps.branch: High Clinical Likelihood or Prior Revascularization
steps.action: Stress imaging (stress echocardiography, CMR, or PET/SPECT MPI) is preferred to document and quantify myocardial ischemia (> 10% LV ischemia triggers invasive angiography).
Initiate first-line antianginal: Beta-blocker (bisoprolol 5 to 10 mg or metoprolol) titrated to resting HR 55 to 60 bpm PLUS high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg) and Aspirin 75 to 100 mg daily.

tables.title: Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy: Antianginal Class Hierarchy and Hemodynamic Tailoring
rows: Beta-blockers (Bisoprolol, Metoprolol succinate)
Lowers HR, lowers BP, reduces myocardial contractility
First-line for all CCS patients, especially post-MI or LVEF <= 40%
Severe bradycardia (HR < 50), high-grade AV block, decompensated acute heart failure, severe asthma
Dihydropyridine CCBs (Amlodipine, Felodipine)
Lowers BP, arterial vasodilation; neutral HR
First-line alternative or combination with beta-blockers; useful in hypertensive angina
Severe aortic stenosis; causes dose-dependent peripheral ankle edema
Non-dihydropyridine CCBs (Diltiazem, Verapamil)
Lowers HR, lowers BP, slows AV conduction
First-line alternative when beta-blockers are contraindicated and LVEF is preserved
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF < 40%), bradycardia, AV block; do not combine with beta-blockers
Long-acting Nitrates (Isosorbide mononitrate)
Venodilation, reduces cardiac preload; neutral HR
Second-line add-on for persistent angina symptoms
Severe aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy; strict absolute contraindication with PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil/tadalafil) within 24 to 48 hours
Metabolic / Late Na Channel Blocker (Ranolazine)
Inhibits late inward sodium current; neutral HR and neutral BP
Second-line add-on in patients with low baseline HR or BP who cannot tolerate beta-blocker titration
End-stage renal disease (CrCl < 30 mL/min), hepatic cirrhosis, baseline severe baseline QT prolongation
tables.caption: Choice of antianginal combination must be personalized to patient baseline heart rate, blood pressure, and left ventricular function.

Pharmacologic nuclear perfusion study; PET is worth considering in morbid obesity or large dense breasts
Dobutamine stress echo or a pharmacologic nuclear study, either is acceptable
Has the patient had coronary revascularization before?
Can the resting ECG be interpreted for ischaemia?
Exercise nuclear study or exercise echo, either is acceptable
